meta.descriptionEn: In November 1988 a Soviet spaceplane lifted off on the super-heavy Energia rocket, circled the Earth twice with nobody on board, and then landed itself on a runway within metres of its target, even while the wind tried to throw it off course. It was a staggering achievement. And then it never flew again. This documentary follows the story of Buran, from the Cold War rivalry with the American Space Shuttle, through the giant Energia rocket and over 1,000 companies building it, to a flight that stunned the world. Why did a perfect success lead nowhere? What happened to the program? And what became of the orbiter sitting in a vast hangar in Kazakhstan?
meta.descriptionUr: Nawambar 1988 mein Soviet Union ka ek spaceplane, Buran, bina kisi insaan ke zameen ke do chakkar laga kar khud hi runway par utar gaya, nishane se sirf chand meter door. Yeh ek hairat angez kamyabi thi, magar iske baad Buran dobara kabhi nahi udaa. Is documentary mein hum Buran aur Energia rocket ki poori kahani dekhenge, American Space Shuttle se muqabla, ek perfect flight, program ka khatma, aur Baikonur ke hangar mein pesh aane wala hadsa. Akhir tak dekhiye aur jaaniye ke itni bari kamyabi ke baad Buran ka kya hua.

articleEn: On 15 November 1988, a spaceplane came down on a runway on the Baikonur steppe with nobody in the cockpit. At 06:24:42 UTC, Buran touched down at Site 251 under its own control. The whole flight was uncrewed. A strong crosswind of 61.2 kilometres per hour was blowing, yet Buran landed just 3 metres sideways and 10 metres lengthwise from the target mark. From launch to landing, the flight took 206 minutes.

Buran was the first spaceplane to fly without a crew and also to land in fully automatic mode. The name means blizzard in Russian. It was the first flight orbiter of the Soviet Buran programme, and its construction number was 1.01.

After this success, though, the story takes a strange turn. Buran never went into space again, so this was its only orbital flight. Then, on 12 May 2002, the roof of a large hangar at Baikonur collapsed. Buran was stored in that hangar, and it was destroyed.

So how did Buran land itself? Why did it never get another chance to fly? And what really happened in that hangar? This is not just the story of one spacecraft. It is the story of a Soviet dream that more than 1,000 companies worked on.

articleEn: To understand the story, we have to look across the ocean. On 12 April 1981, Space Shuttle Columbia made its first flight on the STS-1 mission, flown by John Young and Robert Crippen. The Shuttle was no ordinary rocket. It was the world's first operational orbital spacecraft designed to be reused. It was not fully reusable, however. The orbiter and the solid rocket boosters were reused, but the external tank was the one part that was not. At launch, three RS-25 engines and two boosters fired together, and on return the orbiter glided down to a runway. After STS-4 in 1982, NASA declared the system operational.

Over the years, five orbiters flew a total of 135 missions between 1981 and 2011. Each orbiter was designed for 100 launches or ten years of operational life. The fleet's total mission time came to 1,323 days. Of the 135 missions, 133 returned safely, and the Challenger (1986) and Columbia (2003) accidents killed 14 astronauts in total.

Now look at it from Moscow's side. According to one source, the Soviet government suspected the Shuttle could also be used for military purposes. The US Air Force had a role in the design too, setting requirements of 29,000 kilograms to low Earth orbit and a payload bay of 4.6 by 18 metres.

The Soviet answer was Energia-Buran. According to one source, Energia was built in response to the Shuttle, and its design was largely based on it. The Buran orbiter also resembled the Space Shuttle. Their payload bays were about the same length, 18.55 metres for Buran and 18 metres for the Shuttle. The heat tiles were similar as well. Both orbiters faced similar temperatures, but Buran's tiles were laid out differently on its underside.

One big difference was payload. According to one source, the Space Shuttle could carry at most 30 tonnes to low Earth orbit, while Energia could carry up to 100 tonnes. In that sense the Shuttle is called a heavy-lift vehicle and Energia a super-heavy lift launch vehicle. Soviet engineers chose a different path. The Shuttle programme also proved very expensive: NASA estimates its total budget at about 221 billion dollars in 2012 dollars.
So what did the Soviet Union build in reply? The answer lies in a giant rocket, with Buran attached to its side.

articleEn: Now let us talk about the rocket without which Buran could not have reached space. Its name was Energia, which means energy in Russian. The Energia programme was approved in 1976, after the cancellation of the N1 rocket, which had been built for Soviet crewed lunar missions but never succeeded. Facilities built for N1 were reused, especially the horizontal assembly building at Baikonur's Site 112. In the same way, NASA reused infrastructure built for Saturn V in the Shuttle programme. Energia also replaced a concept called Vulkan, which had been based on Proton.

Energia's first stage had four strap-on boosters. Each had a four-chamber RD-170 engine burning kerosene and liquid oxygen. Each booster was 40 metres tall and 3.9 metres wide, with a burn time of 156 seconds. At the time, the RD-170 was the most powerful liquid-fuel rocket engine. In the middle was the core stage, with four single-chamber RD-0120 engines burning liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen. The core stage was 59 metres tall and 7.75 metres wide, with a burn time of 470 seconds. Development of the control system was led by NPO Electropribor.

Overall, Energia could lift about 100 tonnes to low Earth orbit, 20 tonnes to geostationary orbit and 32 tonnes to a translunar trajectory. An interesting detail is that the payload was mounted not on top but on the side of the rocket, because Energia was fundamentally built for Buran-class orbiters. It had two operational variants. In Energia-Buran, the orbiter itself was the payload. In Buran-T, the payload would travel in a side-mounted cargo container, but that configuration was never flown. Energia was the Soviet Union's first successful super-heavy lift launch vehicle, and the world's second after America's Saturn V.

Now the most important difference. The Space Shuttle's own three RS-25 engines fired during launch, along with solid boosters. Buran's engines were only for orbital manoeuvring. Energia carried it to space, and the orbiter made only a short circularisation burn to reach orbit. Buran's orbital manoeuvring engines had a total thrust of 17,600 kgf, and their specific impulse is given as 362 seconds. Unlike the Shuttle, the Buran orbiter did not provide thrust during launch. All the power came from Energia's four boosters and core stage. One source lists the boosters' vacuum thrust at 7,906 kN and the core stage's at 7,848 kN, which gives an idea of the rocket's scale.
The rocket's design was ready. Now the question was how Buran itself would be built, and how many hands it would take.

articleEn: Construction of Buran began in 1980. By 1984, the first full-scale orbiter had been completed and rolled out. More than 1,000 companies from across the Soviet Union took part in the project. It was not the effort of one city but of the whole country.

The airframe was the orbiter's central structural part, and according to the source, all the other components attached to it. The components needed for flight made up about 20 percent of the weight, while payload systems and removable parts added another 11 percent. As for size, Buran was 36.37 metres long, with a wingspan of 23.92 metres and a height of 16.35 metres on the ground. The payload bay was 18.55 metres long and 4.65 metres in diameter. The maximum payload is given as 30 tonnes and the maximum launch mass as 105 tonnes.

Then came the most delicate part, the heat shield. Buran's underside carried 38,600 carbon-carbon tiles, designed for 100 reentries. They had an antioxidant coating of molybdenum disilicide and were glued to the orbiter, just like the Shuttle's. But the layout was different. The gaps between the tiles were all kept parallel or perpendicular to the airflow. The aim was to keep heat low between the tiles and in the boundary layer, and to maintain laminar airflow around the orbiter. Gaps were deliberately left between tiles for thermal expansion and filled with materials such as quartz fiber and brush seals.

Inside, the crew module was an all-metal, welded, pressurised compartment with three decks. The flight deck at the top was where the commander, pilot, engineer and mission specialist would sit. Its cockpit layout resembled the Shuttle's and had three CRT displays. The middle deck was for living and sleeping, with a galley and toilet. At the bottom, the aggregate compartment housed life support and power systems.

The plan was not just for solo flights. A docking module was also designed, with an APAS-89 docking unit so that Buran could link up with the Mir station. A similar APAS-89 port was fitted to Mir's Kristall module, and the same port was later used in the Shuttle-Mir programme. Like the Shuttle's RMS, an Onboard Manipulator System was also built for Buran, and one or two arms could be fitted depending on the mission. Pressurized laboratory modules like Spacelab were prepared on the 37K design. Two 37KB units were built, and a third was never made because the programme ended.

The early design included two AL-31 jet engines. But in late 1987 or early 1988 it was decided not to install them on flight articles. So more than a thousand companies together built a spaceplane. But could it come back without a pilot on its very first flight?

articleEn: Before Buran could fly, Energia itself had to pass a test. That test came on 15 May 1987. On this first launch the payload was not Buran but the Polyus spacecraft. It was also called Skif-DM, a demonstrator for the Skif orbital weapons platform. Polyus was meant to reach orbit with the help of an FGB, a functional cargo block. This engine section had originally been built for a cancelled Mir module.

Energia's core stage had four RD-0120 engines and its strap-on boosters used RD-170s. This was Energia's first launch. The plan was for the payload to reach an orbit of 280 km altitude and 64.6 degrees inclination, and the final orbital insertion was to be carried out by the payload's own section. On 15 May 1987, Energia flew for the first time. Both stages of the rocket did their part as designed, meaning the boosters and the core stage ran as expected.

So where did the problem arise? The answer was software. There was a software error in the attitude control system, and because of it Polyus's orbital insertion motor could not put the payload into orbit. As a result Polyus re-entered the atmosphere and came down over the Pacific Ocean. The distinction matters here. The launch vehicle did its job, but the payload's final attempt at orbital insertion failed. The failure was the software's, not the rocket's.

After the launch, however, the Soviet Union said something different. At first it was announced as a successful sub-orbital test of the new Energia booster, carrying a dummy payload. Some time later the truth came out. The purpose of the flight had actually been to put Polyus into orbit, not just to run a test. On this flight Polyus took the place of the cargo container. The Buran-T configuration, with its container, was never flown. So the 1987 flight was both a failed mission and a valuable experience for Energia.

The next test was far bigger. Energia was now ready for a second flight. This time it would carry not Polyus but the Buran orbiter itself on its side. And this time nobody would be inside. Could a machine fly to orbit alone and return to Earth? The answer would come on 15 November 1988.

articleEn: At 03:00:02 UTC on 15 November 1988, Energia left the ground at Baikonur with the Buran orbiter on its side. The launch was from Baikonur Cosmodrome's launch pad 110/37. The spaceport is in Kazakhstan today, and Russia operates it under a lease running to 2050. This Energia rocket was number 1L. According to the source, the entire automated launch sequence ran exactly to specification. Remember that the 1987 Polyus rocket was called 6SL, so each Energia launch had its own number.

According to one source, the strap-on boosters burned for 156 seconds and the core stage for 470 seconds, so it was only a few minutes of powerful climb. Energia's distinctive feature was that the payload was mounted on its side, not on top, and Buran's launch followed this design. Energia delivered Buran to a temporary orbit. Then, as planned, the orbiter separated from the rocket. At apogee, Buran made a burn of 66.7 m/s, which put it in a final orbit between 251 km and 263 km. The orbiter completed two circuits of the Earth.

The mission was uncrewed, so there was no commander or pilot aboard. After two orbits, the engines of the ODU, the Combined Propulsion System, fired automatically. This burn started the descent into the atmosphere. From launch to stop, the whole flight lasted 206 minutes, roughly three and a half hours, during which two orbits were completed.

Now look at the payload bay. It held an Accessory Unit called 37KB No.37070, which contained recording equipment and accumulators. The accumulators powered the onboard systems, because the power system based on ordinary fuel cells was not yet ready. Many planned parts were left out of the first flight. The Onboard Manipulator System and the docking module were both missing. And as mentioned earlier, the AL-31 jet engines were not installed for this first orbital flight either. So the orbiter flew without the full configuration of future missions, which is why it is more accurate to call it a test flight.

The flight's code also stands out. Buran's code was 1K1, meaning first orbiter, first flight. It was Energia's second flight, and the first in which the payload successfully reached orbit. After the Polyus failure, that was a big difference.

Was everything fine? The launch was a success and so was the orbit. But the real danger remained, because the orbiter had to land without a pilot. Two orbits of the Earth were done and the engine burn was complete. Now all eyes were on Site 251 and the automatic landing system.

articleEn: After the ODU engine burn, Buran began its return. It now had to descend from 100 kilometres altitude without any pilot. Its automatic landing system could handle descent, approach and landing from any point within its predefined acceptable area. On this descent Buran had to cover 8,000 kilometres through the air, and its speed had to fall from 28,000 kilometres per hour to zero.

On the Space Shuttle it was different. There, GPCs flew the reentry, but once the orbiter reached subsonic speed the crew took manual control. Buran's cockpit layout resembled the Shuttle's, with three CRT displays. On this flight, though, the machine had to make the decisions itself.

Now comes the part that made this flight stand out. At an altitude of 20 kilometres there was a key point, and there the system did something unexpected. Normally the approach came from the south, with two left turns needed to reach the final course. That was the standard method. But this time the system made extra turns in both directions. Buran passed over the field to the north, then turned right and came onto the final course. The chance of such a manoeuvre is estimated at only 3 percent.

Why did the system do this? Had something broken? No. The reason was strong, gusty wind. At ground level the wind was 15 metres per second, with gusts reaching 20 metres per second. Because of this wind, the orbiter's energy had not fallen as much as it should have. The extra turns lengthened the glide and shed the surplus energy. In other words, the computer changed its route to suit the conditions. It was one of the most remarkable moments of the flight.

Then came touchdown. At 06:24:42 UTC, Buran landed on the Site 251 runway under its own control, and it came to a complete stop at 06:25:24. A crosswind of 61.2 kilometres per hour was blowing at the time. Even so, Buran stopped only 3 metres to the side and 10 metres along the runway from the target mark. From launch to landing, 206 minutes had passed. It was the first spaceplane to fly without a crew and also to land in fully automatic mode.

A later inspection found that 8 of Buran's 38,000 thermal tiles had come off during the flight. One small note: in the source, the figure 38,600 refers to the tiles on the orbiter's underside, while 38,000 appears in the description of the tile losses.
So a machine landed itself and showed what it could do. But the real question now begins: after such a brilliant success, why was there no second flight?

articleEn: After Buran's successful flight, talk turned to the next step. In 1989 it was estimated that Buran's second uncrewed flight would take place by 1993. That flight was expected to last 15 to 20 days, a much longer mission than the short first flight of just two orbits. But the plan was never fulfilled. The Soviet Union collapsed, funding dried up, and in 1993 the Buran programme was formally ended. With it, Energia's story ended too. The rocket made only two flights: with Polyus in 1987 and with Buran in 1988. Work on Energia began in 1976, and the programme was formally closed in 1993.

The Space Shuttle kept flying during this time and afterwards, until 2011. Its programme ran for 30 years, from 1981 to 2011, and flew 135 missions. Buran got only one flight. Energia could lift about 100 tonnes to low Earth orbit, while the Space Shuttle could lift at most 30 tonnes. Yet despite that power, Energia got only two flights.

Three major Energia variants had been imagined. The smallest was Energia-M, with two boosters instead of four and one RD-0120 engine in the core. It was meant to replace Proton, but in a 1993 competition the Angara rocket won. A non-functional prototype of Energia-M still exists at Baikonur. Energia-2 was a fully reusable concept. The largest was Vulkan, with eight Block A boosters and a target of up to 200 tonnes. Work on Vulkan and preparation of site 250 continued from 1990 to 1993. Then, with a lack of funds and the collapse of the Soviet Union, it was abandoned.

One part of Energia survived, though: its RD-170 engine. In its time it was the most powerful rocket engine to use liquid fuel. A close version of it was used in the Zenit rocket, which flew until 2017. The half-size RD-180 powered America's Atlas III and Atlas V. The RD-191 is linked to Angara and Naro-1, while the RD-181, based on the RD-191, was used in Antares 200.

In 2016, Roscosmos announced conceptual plans to build a super heavy-lift rocket from Energia parts, especially the RD-171 engine. In September 2021, tests of the updated RD-171MV engine were completed, which could possibly be used in the Soyuz-5 rocket. Rumours of Energia production restarting kept circulating, but the source calls this very unlikely. So what became of the orbiter that was left?

chapters.covers: Buran stored in MIK 112 at Baikonur, a hangar built in late 1960s for the lunar programme. Roof collapse 12 May 2002 fell roughly 220-260 feet, destroying Buran and an Energia test article, killing at least six workers, two presumed dead, a safety engineer died of heart failure. Terrorism ruled out; early theory of heavy object falling on an Energia fuel tank. Starsem clean rooms unusable. Remains scrapped. Baikonur context. Conclusion: what Buran proved (automation, a spaceplane flying itself), what was lost, open questions, lessons, Shuttle's ending in 2011 and its parts reused for Artemis versus Buran's fate; request to like and subscribe.

articleEn: 12 May 2002. After the programme ended, Buran was kept at Baikonur's Rocket Assembly and Fueling Facility, known as MIK 112. This large hangar was built in the late 1960s for the Soviet lunar programme and was later used for the Buran programme. On that day the building's roof suddenly collapsed. According to sources it fell from a height of roughly 220 to 260 feet. Buran was destroyed in the accident, along with an Energia test article. Another source says all the remaining Energia core stages were destroyed as well.

At least six construction workers died in the disaster, and two more were believed to have died too. A safety engineer also died of heart failure a short time after the incident. We offer our sympathy to all of their families.

Was it sabotage? Officials of the Russian space agency said terrorism had been ruled out. Early investigations produced one theory: some people thought a heavy object had fallen onto one of three protected Energia fuel tanks. The same building also held Starsem clean rooms for commercial Soyuz missions. They were not destroyed but became unusable. The wreckage of Buran and Energia was later cleared away and scrapped. So the only orbiter that had gone into space was gone forever.

Baikonur is the cosmodrome from which Sputnik 1 and Vostok 1 flew, and whose foundation was laid in 1955. Buran showed that a spaceplane could return from space without a crew and land by itself. Its landing was only 3 and 10 metres from the target. But what was lost was also significant: an orbiter, a whole programme, and the second flight that never happened.

The Space Shuttle's end was different. On 21 July 2011, Atlantis completed the final flight, and the remaining orbiters were placed in museums. Their engines and boosters are being reused in the Artemis programme, and parts of Artemis I had already flown on 83 Shuttle missions. So, friends, Buran's story is the story of a success that never got the chance to move forward. If you liked the video, like and subscribe.

shorts.titleEn: The Spaceplane That Landed With Nobody Inside
shorts.text: ایک spaceplane runway پر اترا، اور اس کے cockpit میں کوئی انسان نہیں تھا! 15 November 1988 کو Buran نے Site 251 پر اپنے ہی control میں touchdown کیا۔ وقت تھا 06:24:42 UTC۔ باہر 61.2 کلومیٹر فی گھنٹہ کی crosswind چل رہی تھی۔ پھر بھی Buran اپنے target mark سے صرف 3 میٹر lateral اور 10 میٹر longitudinal فاصلے پر رکا۔ launch سے landing تک کل 206 منٹ لگے۔ یہ پہلا spaceplane تھا جس نے بغیر crew کے پرواز کی اور fully automatic mode میں land بھی کیا۔ Buran کا مطلب Russian میں blizzard ہے، یعنی برفانی طوفان۔ مگر کیا یہ کامیابی کسی کو آگے لے جا سکی؟ اس کا جواب بہت تلخ ہے۔ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek spaceplane runway par utra, aur is ke cockpit mein koi insaan nahin tha! 15 November 1988 ko Buran ne Site 251 par apne hi control mein touchdown kiya. Waqt tha 06:24:42 UTC. Bahar 61.2 kilometre fi ghanta ki crosswind chal rahi thi. Phir bhi Buran apne target mark se sirf 3 meter lateral aur 10 meter longitudinal faasle par ruka. Launch se landing tak kul 206 minute lagay. Yeh pehla spaceplane tha jis ne baghair crew ke parwaz ki aur fully automatic mode mein land bhi kiya. Buran ka matlab Russian mein blizzard hai, yaani barfani toofan. Magar kya yeh kamyabi kisi ko aagay le ja saki? Is ka jawab bohat talkh hai. Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
Buran touched down on its own in 1988 with no crew aboard, landing within metres of its target in strong crosswind.
A look at the first fully automatic spaceplane landing.

shorts.titleEn: The 3% Move: How Buran's Computer Saved Its Landing
shorts.text: ایک computer نے آخری لمحے میں ایسا فیصلہ کیا جس کا امکان صرف 3 فیصد تھا! Buran کا automatic landing system 100 کلومیٹر کی بلندی سے descent شروع کر کے فضا میں 8,000 کلومیٹر کا سفر طے کرتا رہا۔ رفتار 28,000 کلومیٹر فی گھنٹہ سے گھٹ کر صفر تک آنی تھی۔ پھر 20 کلومیٹر کے key point پر system نے غیر معمولی maneuver چنا۔ عام approach جنوب سے تھی، مگر Buran نے دونوں طرف اضافی turns لیے اور field کے شمال سے گزرا۔ وجہ تھی تیز جھکڑ والی ہوا، جو 15 میٹر فی سیکنڈ تھی اور gusts 20 تک جاتی تھیں۔ توانائی کم نہیں ہو رہی تھی۔ تو کیا یہ چال کامیاب رہی؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek computer ne aakhri lamhay mein aisa faisla kiya jis ka imkan sirf 3 feesad tha! Buran ka automatic landing system 100 kilometre ki bulandi se descent shuru kar ke fiza mein 8,000 kilometre ka safar tay karta raha. Raftaar 28,000 kilometre fi ghanta se ghat kar sifar tak aani thi. Phir 20 kilometre ke key point par system ne ghair mamooli maneuver chuna. Aam approach junoob se thi, magar Buran ne donon taraf izafi turns liye aur field ke shumal se guzra. Wajah thi tez jhakkar wali hawa, jo 15 meter fi second thi aur gusts 20 tak jati thin. Tawanai kam nahin ho rahi thi. To kya yeh chaal kamyab rahi? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.

shorts.roman: 12 May 2002 ko ek chhat giri aur Buran hamesha ke liye khatam ho gaya! Program khatam honay ke baad ise Baikonur ke MIK 112 hangar mein rakha gaya tha. Yeh bara hangar 1960 ki dahai ke aakhir mein Soviet lunar programme ke liye bana tha. Phir imarat ki chhat taqriban 220 se 260 feet ki bulandi se neeche aa giri. Is hadsay mein Buran aur ek Energia test article tabah ho gaye. Kam az kam 6 tameerati mazdoor apni jaan se gaye. Hum un ke khandanon ke gham mein shareek hain. To aakhir chhat giri kyun? In 2002 the roof of Baikonur's MIK 112 hangar collapsed, destroying the only space-flown Buran orbiter.
We also remember the workers who were lost in the collapse.
